key_terms.meaning: A function of an independent variable that carries information, written x(t) in continuous time or x[n] in discrete time.
A signal defined for every real value of time t, such as x(t)=sin(2πft).
A signal defined only at integer index n, such as x[n]=0.8ⁿ for n≥0.
Each value x[n] of a discrete-time signal; for a sampled signal x[n] = x(nTₛ), where Tₛ is the sampling interval.
An operator that maps an input signal x to an output signal y, written y=T{x}.
An energy signal has finite nonzero E = ∫|x(t)|²dt and P = 0; a power signal has finite nonzero P = lim (1/T)∫|x(t)|²dt over a window of length T centred on 0, and E = ∞.
A signal that repeats after a period T>0, so x(t+T)=x(t) for all t; the smallest such T is the fundamental period.
x(t) is even if x(−t)=x(t), odd if x(−t)=−x(t); every signal splits into even plus odd parts.
δ(t) is a generalized pulse with unit area, δ(t)=0 for t≠0 and ∫δ(t)dt=1; in discrete time δ[n]=1 at n=0 and 0 elsewhere.
u(t) = 0 for t < 0 and 1 for t ≥ 0 (this book takes u(0) = 1); in discrete time u[n] = 1 for n ≥ 0 and 0 for n < 0.
r(t)=t u(t), zero for t<0 and rising linearly for t≥0; in discrete time r[n]=n u[n].
x(t) = A e<sup>st</sup>, where A is the amplitude and s = σ + jω; real s gives growth or decay, imaginary s gives a sinusoid.
sgn(t) = 2u(t) − 1 (t ≠ 0); rect(t/τ) = u(t + τ/2) − u(t − τ/2); sinc(t) = sin(πt)/(πt).
Replacing x(t) by x(t−t₀) moves the signal right by t₀ when t₀>0.
Replacing x(t) by x(at) compresses the signal in time when |a|>1 and stretches it when 0<|a|<1.
Replacing x(t) by x(−t) flips the signal about t=0.
The output at each instant uses only the input at that instant, such as y(t) = 3x(t) + 2.
A system is linear if it obeys superposition: T{a x₁+b x₂}=a T{x₁}+b T{x₂} for all inputs and constants.
A system is time-invariant if a delayed input gives the same output delayed by the same amount: x(t−t₀)→y(t−t₀).
A system is causal if its output at any time depends only on present and past inputs, not future inputs.
A system is bounded-input bounded-output stable if every bounded input produces a bounded output.
Two signals are orthogonal on an interval if their inner product is zero, ∫x(t)y*(t)dt=0; such signals can form a basis.
c₁₂ = ∫f₁f₂ dt / ∫f₂² dt, the multiple of f₂ that leaves the least error energy.
cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩/Kₙ, where Kₙ = ‖φₙ‖² is the energy of φₙ.
A set whose N-term error energy tends to 0 for every finite-energy signal; then x = Σcₙφₙ.
∫|x(t)|²dt = Σ|cₙ|²Kₙ; for a periodic signal P = Σ|Dₙ|² = a₀² + Σ(aₙ² + bₙ²)/2.

takeaways: A signal is a function of an independent variable that carries information, and a system maps input signals to output signals.
Continuous-time signals use real t and discrete-time signals use integer n; sampling gives x[n] = x(nTₛ), but many DT signals are discrete by nature.
Energy and power classify signals by finite energy or finite nonzero average power, while periodic, even, and odd properties simplify later work.
The impulse, step, ramp, and exponential are standard building blocks and common test inputs for systems.
Operations on the independent variable change the graph: shifting moves it, scaling compresses or stretches it, and reversal flips it.
A system is CT or DT by the variable of its input and output, and its properties must be tested from definitions.
Linearity, time invariance, causality, and BIBO stability are separate tests; one does not automatically imply another.
Signals on an interval behave like vectors: the inner product measures how much of one lies along another, and c₁₂ = ⟨f₁, f₂⟩/‖f₂‖² gives the best approximation.
In an orthogonal set each coefficient is one inner product, cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩/Kₙ, found without the others.
A complete orthogonal set drives the error energy to zero, and Parseval's relation E = Σ|cₙ|²Kₙ splits the energy among the terms.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for precise definitions with sketches, the classification of a given signal, operations such as x(at − b) and the four system-property tests. Most syllabi that teach the vector view also ask for the component of one signal along another, and for Parseval's relation with a complete orthogonal set.

bank.q: Define a signal and a system. Distinguish continuous-time and discrete-time signals with one example and one sketch description for each.
outline: Signal: a function of an independent variable that carries information
System: an operator mapping an input signal to an output signal
CT uses real t, DT uses integer n
Examples: x(t) = 4 sin(20πt) V and its samples x[n] = 4 sin(0.2πn) V
Sketch: continuous curve against stem plot
answer: Signal. A signal is a function of an independent variable that carries information. The value at one instant is the amplitude and carries units: volts on a microphone lead, °C from a temperature sensor, rupees for a share price.
System. A system is an operator T that maps an input signal to an output signal, y(t) = T{x(t)} or y[n] = T{x[n]}. Example: an amplifier with y(t) = 100 x(t) turns a 20 mV input into 2 V.

Continuous-time (CT) signal. The independent variable t is a real number, so x(t) has a value at every instant. Example: a vibration sensor voltage x(t) = 4 sin(20πt) V, with period 2π/(20π) = 0.1 s. Sketch: a smooth sine curve against t in seconds, peaks of 4 V at t = 0.025 s and 0.125 s, a trough of −4 V at t = 0.075 s, crossing zero every 0.05 s.

Discrete-time (DT) signal. The independent variable n is an integer, so x[n] exists only at n = …, −1, 0, 1, 2, … Example: sampling the same voltage every Tₛ = 10 ms gives x[n] = x(0.01n) = 4 sin(0.2πn) V. Sketch: vertical stems at integer n with a dot on top: x[0] = 0, x[1] = 2.35 V, x[2] = 3.80 V, x[5] = 0, x[7] = −3.80 V. Nothing is drawn between the stems, because nothing is defined at n = 2.5.

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Feature
CT signal
DT signal
rows: sampler output, daily counts, log files
Fourier series and transform, Laplace transform

answer: A DT signal need not come from sampling. The number of UPI transactions completed each day is discrete by nature, and so is a sequence defined by a formula. Sampling is one route from CT to DT, given by x[n] = x(nTₛ).
Systems take the same labels: an RC low-pass filter with voltage in and voltage out is a CT system; a five-point moving average on stored samples is a DT system.
Check: x[2] = 4 sin(0.4π) = 4 × 0.951 = 3.80 V, and x(0.02 s) = 4 sin(20π × 0.02) = 4 sin(0.4π) = 3.80 V, so the sample equals the CT value at t = 2Tₛ.

bank.q: Classify a signal by energy, power, periodicity, and even or odd symmetry. Give the defining equation and one test for each class.
outline: Energy E = ∫|x(t)|²dt; energy signal when 0 < E < ∞
Power P = lim (1/T)∫|x(t)|²dt over a window of length T; power signal when 0 < P < ∞
Periodic test x(t + T) = x(t); fundamental period is the smallest T
Even test x(−t) = x(t), odd test x(−t) = −x(t)
Even and odd decomposition formula

answer.text: Energy. The total energy (normalised to 1 Ω) is
answer.pre: E = ∫ |x(t)|² dt  over all t        (DT: E = Σ |x[n]|² over all n)

answer: An energy signal has 0 < E < ∞, and then P = 0. Test: x(t) = e−2tu(t) V gives E = ∫ e−4t dt from 0 to ∞ = 1/4 J. It is finite, so x is an energy signal.

answer.text: Power. The average power over a window of length T centred on zero, as T grows, is
answer.pre: P = lim (T → ∞) (1/T) ∫ |x(t)|² dt,  over −T/2 ≤ t ≤ T/2

answer: A power signal has 0 < P < ∞, and then E = ∞. Test: x(t) = 6 cos(200πt) + 3 V. The cosine contributes 6²/2 = 18 W, the constant 3² = 9 W and the cross term averages to zero, so P = 27 W: a power signal. A signal can be neither: x(t) = t gives ∫ t² dt over −T/2 to T/2 = T³/12, so P = lim T²/12 = ∞ and E = ∞.

answer.text: Periodicity. x is periodic when a positive shift leaves it unchanged; the smallest such shift is the fundamental period T₀.
answer.pre: x(t + T) = x(t) for all t        (DT: x[n + N] = x[n], N a positive integer)

answer: Tests: 6 cos(200πt) + 3 has T₀ = 2π/(200π) = 0.01 s. x[n] = cos(0.2πn) has Ω/(2π) = 0.1 = 1/10, rational, so N₀ = 10. x[n] = cos(2n) has Ω/(2π) = 1/π, irrational, so it is not periodic. A CT sum is periodic only when the ratio of periods is rational: cos(2πt) + cos(3πt) has periods 1 s and 2/3 s, ratio 3/2, and T₀ = 2 s.

answer.text: Even and odd.
answer.pre:
even: x(−t) = x(t)        odd: x(−t) = −x(t)
xₑ(t) = (x(t) + x(−t))/2     xₒ(t) = (x(t) − x(−t))/2

answer: Test: x(t) = 5 + 3t gives x(−t) = 5 − 3t, so xₑ(t) = 5 and xₒ(t) = 3t. Neither part is zero, so x is neither even nor odd. An odd signal must have x(0) = 0; here x(0) = 5.

answer.text: Summary.

answer: Check: the even and odd parts carry the energy between them. For x[n] = 1, 2, 3 at n = 0, 1, 2, Eₑ = 7.5 and Eₒ = 6.5 add to E = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14.

bank.q: Define the unit impulse, unit step, ramp, and exponential signals. State the relations among impulse, step, and ramp in continuous time.
outline: Impulse: zero except at the origin, unit area, sifting property
Step: zero before the origin, one from the origin on
Ramp: r(t) = t u(t)
Exponential: A e<sup>at</sup> real, e<sup>jωt</sup> complex
Relations: the step is the integral of the impulse, the ramp the integral of the step; differentiation walks back
answer: Unit impulse. δ(t) = 0 for t ≠ 0 and ∫ δ(t) dt = 1 over all t. It is not an ordinary function: only its area and its sifting action are defined, ∫ x(t) δ(t − t₀) dt = x(t₀) for x continuous at t₀. Scaling rule: δ(at) = δ(t)/|a|. In DT, δ[n] = 1 at n = 0 and 0 elsewhere.
Unit step. u(t) = 0 for t < 0 and 1 for t ≥ 0 (this book takes u(0) = 1). In DT, u[n] = 1 for n ≥ 0 and 0 for n < 0. It models a switch closing at t = 0; u(t − a) switches on at t = a.
Unit ramp. r(t) = t u(t): zero for t < 0 and equal to t for t ≥ 0. In DT, r[n] = n u[n]. It models a quantity rising at a steady rate.
Exponential. Real: x(t) = A eatu(t); it decays for a < 0 with time constant 1/|a|, grows for a > 0 and is constant for a = 0. Complex: ejωt = cos ωt + j sin ωt, with ω in rad/s.

answer.text: Relations in continuous time. Each signal is the running integral of the one before it, and the derivative steps back down the chain:
answer.pre:
u(t) = ∫ δ(τ) dτ  over −∞ < τ ≤ t        δ(t) = du/dt
r(t) = ∫ u(τ) dτ  over −∞ < τ ≤ t        u(t) = dr/dt
chain:  δ(t) → u(t) → r(t) → (t²/2) u(t)

answer: In DT the same relations use sums and differences: u[n] = Σ δ[k] for k ≤ n, δ[n] = u[n] − u[n − 1], and r[n] = n u[n].

answer.text: Values at a glance.

answer: Use of the relations: x(t) = 2u(t + 1) − 3u(t − 2) + 4e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t) V differentiates to dx/dt = 2δ(t + 1) − 3δ(t − 2) + 4δ(t) − 8e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t) V/s. Each jump gives an impulse whose area is the jump height; the product rule gives the 4δ(t) from the exponential switching on.

Sifting and scaling in use: ∫ (t² + 1) δ(t − 2) dt = 2² + 1 = 5, because the impulse picks the value at t = 2; δ(2t − 4) = δ(2(t − 2)) = (1/2)δ(t − 2), because the area of an impulse squeezed by 2 halves.

Exponential in numbers: e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t) has time constant 1/2 = 0.5 s; after 0.5 s it has fallen to e<sup>−1</sup> = 0.368 of its start, after 2.5 s (five time constants) to e<sup>−5</sup> = 0.0067, which is why engineers treat it as finished after about five time constants.
Check: r(3) = 3, and ∫ u(τ) dτ from −∞ to 3 is the area of a unit-height strip from 0 to 3, which is 3. The two agree.

bank.q: Explain time shifting, time scaling, and time reversal on x(t). For y(t) = x(2t − 6), state the correct order of operations.
outline: x(t − t₀) shifts right for t₀ > 0
x(at) compresses for |a| > 1 and stretches for 0 < |a| < 1
x(−t) reverses about t = 0
x(2t − 6) = x(2(t − 3)): scale by 2, then shift right by 3
Equivalent order: shift right by 6, then scale by 2
answer: Take a concrete signal: x(t) = 2 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 s and 0 elsewhere, a pulse of height 2 and width 2 s.

Time shifting. y(t) = x(t − t₀) moves every feature from t₁ to t₁ + t₀. For t₀ > 0 the signal is delayed (moves right); for t₀ < 0 it is advanced. x(t − 3) is the pulse on 3 to 5 s. Shape and height do not change.
Time scaling. y(t) = x(at) moves a feature from t₁ to t₁/a. For |a| > 1 the signal is compressed, for 0 < |a| < 1 it is stretched. x(2t) is the pulse on 0 to 1 s, width 2/2 = 1 s.
Time reversal. y(t) = x(−t) mirrors the signal about t = 0: x(−t) is the pulse on −2 to 0 s. It is not −x(t), which would flip the amplitude to −2.
Order for x(2t − 6). Write it as x(2(t − 3)). Recipe A: scale first, x(t) → x(2t) on 0 to 1 s; then replace t by t − 3, giving x(2(t − 3)) on 3 to 4 s. The shift after scaling is b/a = 6/2 = 3 s.
Recipe B: shift first by the full 6 s, x(t) → x(t − 6) on 6 to 8 s; then replace t by 2t, giving x(2t − 6) on 3 to 4 s. Both recipes agree.
The usual mistake is to shift by 3 s first and then scale: x(t − 3) → x(2t − 3), which is the pulse on 1.5 to 2.5 s, the wrong signal.

answer.text: Edge check by solving the inequality for the nonzero part:
Summary.

answer: Sketch description: three rows on one time axis. Row 1, x(t), a rectangle of height 2 from 0 to 2 s. Row 2, x(2t), the same height from 0 to 1 s. Row 3, x(2t − 6), the same height from 3 to 4 s. The width halves once (scaling) and the left edge moves from 0 to 3 s (the shift b/a).
Reversal combines the same way: x(−2t + 6) = x(−2(t − 3)) is x(2t) reversed (on −1 to 0 s) and then delayed by 3 s, giving the pulse on 2 to 3 s. Check: 0 ≤ −2t + 6 ≤ 2 gives 2 ≤ t ≤ 3.
Check: at t = 3.5 s the argument is 2(3.5) − 6 = 1, inside 0 to 2, so y(3.5) = x(1) = 2; at t = 2.5 s the argument is −1, outside, so y(2.5) = 0. Both match the interval 3 to 4 s.

bank.q: Define a continuous-time system and a discrete-time system. Give one electrical example of each and identify input and output.
outline: CT system: input x(t) gives output y(t) for real t
DT system: input x[n] gives output y[n] for integer n
CT example: RC low-pass filter with voltage input and output
DT example: a digital filter acting on samples
State input and output clearly
answer: CT system. A system whose input and output are continuous-time signals: y(t) = T{x(t)}, with t real. It is usually described by a differential equation.
DT system. A system whose input and output are discrete-time signals: y[n] = T{x[n]}, with n an integer. It is usually described by a difference equation and runs on a processor.

answer.text: Electrical CT example: RC low-pass filter. Input: the source voltage x(t) across the series R and C. Output: the capacitor voltage y(t). Kirchhoff's voltage law gives
answer.pre: RC dy/dt + y(t) = x(t)

answer: With R = 1 kΩ and C = 1 µF, the time constant is RC = 1 ms. For a 1 V step input starting from rest, y(t) = 1 − e<sup>−t/RC</sup> V, so y(1 ms) = 1 − e<sup>−1</sup> = 0.632 V. Both signals exist at every real t, so the system is CT.

answer.text: Electrical DT example: two-point averaging filter. An ADC samples a voltage; a microcontroller computes
Input: the samples x[n] in volts. Output: the samples y[n] in volts, sent to a DAC. With x[n] = 0, 2, 4, 6 V for n = 0 to 3 and x[−1] = 0:

answer: The label comes from the independent variable, not the hardware: the ADC before this filter is a hybrid CT-to-DT block, and the filter itself is DT.

answer.text: CT and DT systems side by side:

head: Feature
RC low-pass filter (CT)
Two-point average (DT)
rows: yes: one past sample is stored
0.5 V at n = 0, then 1 V from n = 1

answer: Check: y[2] = 0.5(4) + 0.5(2) = 3 V, the average of the two most recent samples.

bank.q: Given x(t) = u(t + 1) − u(t − 2), sketch x(t), find its even and odd parts, and state whether it is an energy or power signal.
outline: Pulse of height 1 from t = −1 to t = 2
Even part xₑ(t) = [x(t) + x(−t)]/2
Odd part xₒ(t) = [x(t) − x(−t)]/2
Energy E = ∫|x(t)|²dt = 3
Finite energy: energy signal, average power zero
answer: Sketch x(t). u(t + 1) switches on at t = −1 and u(t − 2) switches on at t = 2. Their difference is 1 for −1 ≤ t < 2 and 0 elsewhere: a pulse of height 1 and width 3 s.
Reverse. x(−t) = u(−t + 1) − u(−t − 2) is 1 for −2 < t ≤ 1 and 0 elsewhere: the same pulse mirrored about t = 0.

svg.aria: Three sketches: x(t) is 1 from t = −1 to 2; its even part is 0.5 on −2 to −1, 1 on −1 to 1 and 0.5 on 1 to 2; its odd part is −0.5 on −2 to −1, 0 on −1 to 1 and 0.5 on 1 to 2.

answer: In step form: xₑ(t) = 0.5[u(t + 2) + u(t + 1) − u(t − 1) − u(t − 2)] and xₒ(t) = 0.5[−u(t + 2) + u(t + 1) + u(t − 1) − u(t − 2)]. Adding them gives u(t + 1) − u(t − 2) = x(t).
Symmetry check: xₑ(−1.5) = xₑ(1.5) = 0.5, so xₑ is even; xₒ(−1.5) = −0.5 = −xₒ(1.5), so xₒ is odd.

answer.text: Energy and power.
answer.pre:
E = ∫ |x(t)|² dt = ∫ 1 dt over −1 ≤ t ≤ 2 = 3
P = lim (T → ∞) E/T = lim 3/T = 0

answer: E = 3 is finite and nonzero and P = 0, so x(t) is an energy signal (3 J if x is a voltage across 1 Ω).

Sketch description: three rows on one time axis from −3 to 3 s. x(t) is a single block of height 1 from −1 to 2. xₑ(t) is a symmetric staircase: 0.5 on −2 to −1, 1 on −1 to 1, 0.5 on 1 to 2. xₒ(t) is −0.5 on −2 to −1, zero on −1 to 1 and +0.5 on 1 to 2, a mirror image with a sign change.

Why the energies add: xₑ(t)xₒ(t) is (0.5)(−0.5) = −0.25 on −2 to −1, 0 on −1 to 1 and (0.5)(0.5) = 0.25 on 1 to 2, so ∫ xₑxₒ dt = −0.25 + 0 + 0.25 = 0. The cross term in E = ∫ (xₑ + xₒ)² dt vanishes, leaving Eₑ + Eₒ. The same holds for every signal, because an even times an odd function is odd and integrates to zero over a symmetric range.
Check: Eₑ = (0.5)²(1) + (1)²(2) + (0.5)²(1) = 0.25 + 2 + 0.25 = 2.5 and Eₒ = (0.5)²(1) + (0.5)²(1) = 0.5. Eₑ + Eₒ = 3 = E, as it must be, because the even and odd parts are orthogonal.

bank.q: Using unit step functions, write a rectangular pulse p(t) of height A and width W centred at t = 0. Sketch p(2t + 4) and p(−t + 1).
outline: p(2t + 4) = p(2(t + 2)): centre at t = −2 and width W/2
p(−t + 1) = p(−(t − 1)): centre at t = 1 and width W
Amplitude A in both sketches
Step functions mark the edges
answer: The pulse. The pulse switches on at t = −W/2 and off at t = W/2, so p(t) = A[u(t + W/2) − u(t − W/2)]. It is even, with area A·W.

answer.text: p(2t + 4). Write it as p(2(t + 2)): compress by 2, then shift left by 2. Edges from the inequality:

answer: So p(2t + 4) = A[u(t + 2 + W/4) − u(t + 2 − W/4)]: centre t = −2, width W/2, height A.

answer.text: p(−t + 1). Write it as p(−(t − 1)): reverse, then shift right by 1. Edges:

answer: So p(−t + 1) = A[u(t − 1 + W/2) − u(t − 1 − W/2)]: centre t = 1, width W, height A. Reversal does not change an even pulse; only the shift shows.

answer.text: With numbers, A = 3 and W = 4:

answer: Sketch description: three rectangles of height 3 on one time axis. p(t) spans −2 to 2; p(2t + 4) is half as wide, spanning −3 to −1; p(−t + 1) has the original width and spans −1 to 3.

General rule from the two results: for x(at + b) a pulse of width W centred at 0 moves to centre −b/a and takes width W/|a|. For p(2t + 4): centre −4/2 = −2, width 4/2 = 2. For p(−t + 1): centre −1/(−1) = 1, width 4/1 = 4.
Area check: the area of p(2t + 4) is 3 × 2 = 6, half the area 3 × 4 = 12 of p(t), because compressing time by 2 halves every area. Reversal and shifting keep the area, so p(−t + 1) still has area 12.

Check: at t = −2 the argument of p(2t + 4) is 0, the centre of p, so the value is 3. At t = 1 the argument of p(−t + 1) is 0, again the centre, so the value is 3. At t = 0, p(2t + 4) = p(4) = 0, since 4 is outside −2 to 2.

bank.q: Test the system y(t) = t x(t) for linearity, time invariance, causality, and BIBO stability. Show the steps.
outline: Linearity: T{a x₁ + b x₂} = t(a x₁ + b x₂) = a y₁ + b y₂
Time invariance: input x(t − t₀) gives t x(t − t₀), not (t − t₀)x(t − t₀)
Causality: output at t uses input at the same t only
Stability: bounded |x| ≤ M gives |y| ≤ M|t|, unbounded as |t| → ∞
Conclusion: linear, time-varying, causal, not BIBO stable

answer.text: Linearity. Apply the input a x₁(t) + b x₂(t):
answer.pre:
T{a x₁ + b x₂} = t[a x₁(t) + b x₂(t)]
               = a·t x₁(t) + b·t x₂(t)
               = a y₁(t) + b y₂(t)

answer: Additivity and scaling both hold for all inputs and constants, so the system is linear. It also gives zero output for zero input, as every linear system must.

answer.text: Time invariance. Delay the input by t₀ and compare with the delayed output:
answer.pre:
input x(t − t₀)       → output y₁(t) = t x(t − t₀)
delayed output        → y(t − t₀) = (t − t₀) x(t − t₀)

answer: These differ whenever t₀ ≠ 0. Numbers: x(t) = 2 V, t₀ = 1 s, t = 2 s. y₁(2) = 2 × 2 = 4 V·s, but y(2 − 1) = (2 − 1) × 2 = 2 V·s. One counterexample is enough: the system is time-varying. The coefficient t means the gain depends on when the input arrives.
Causality. The output at time t uses x(t) at that same instant only, never x at a later time. The system is causal (and memoryless).

BIBO stability. Take the bounded input x(t) = 2 V, so |x(t)| ≤ Mᵢₙ = 2 V. Then y(t) = 2t V·s, and |y(t)| = 2|t| grows without limit as |t| → ∞. No finite Mₒᵤₜ bounds the output, so the system is not BIBO stable.

answer.text: Trace of the numbers used:
Result.

head: Property
Result
Reason
rows: 4 V·s ≠ 2 V·s at t = 2 s with t₀ = 1 s
uses x at the present instant only

answer: A numeric linearity check: at t = 3 s, inputs x₁ = 1 V and x₂ = 2 V give y₁ = 3 and y₂ = 6 V·s; the input x₁ + x₂ = 3 V gives 3 × 3 = 9 V·s = y₁ + y₂, and the input 5x₁ = 5 V gives 15 V·s = 5y₁.

Why a constant input is a fair test of time invariance: a delayed constant is the same constant, so a time-invariant system would have to give the same output after the delay, shifted by 1 s. Here the output for the same input is 2t before and 2t after, but the shifted output should be 2(t − 1); the gain t depends on the clock, which is exactly what time-varying means.

A pulse input shows the same thing: x(t) = u(t) − u(t − 1) gives y = t on 0 to 1 s (peak 1 V·s), but the delayed pulse x(t − 1) gives y = t on 1 to 2 s (peak 2 V·s), a taller output, not a shifted copy.
Check: the properties are independent, so a linear causal system can still be time-varying and unstable. At t = 10 s, y = 10 s × 2 V = 20 V·s, as y = t·x says.

bank.q: Test the discrete-time system y[n] = x[n] + x[n − 1] for linearity, time invariance, causality, and BIBO stability. Justify each answer.
outline: Linearity follows from addition and scaling
Time invariance: a delayed input gives the same output delayed
Causality: uses present and past input only
Stability: |y[n]| ≤ |x[n]| + |x[n − 1]| ≤ 2M for bounded input
Conclusion: linear, time-invariant, causal, BIBO stable

answer.text: Linearity.
answer.pre:
T{a x₁ + b x₂} = (a x₁[n] + b x₂[n]) + (a x₁[n − 1] + b x₂[n − 1])
               = a(x₁[n] + x₁[n − 1]) + b(x₂[n] + x₂[n − 1])
               = a y₁[n] + b y₂[n]

answer: Superposition holds, so the system is linear.

answer.text: Time invariance. Feed x₁[n] = x[n − n₀]:
answer.pre:
T{x[n − n₀]} = x[n − n₀] + x[n − n₀ − 1]
y[n − n₀]    = x[n − n₀] + x[n − 1 − n₀]

answer: The two are equal for every integer n₀, so the system is time-invariant. Its coefficients (1 and 1) do not depend on n.

answer.text: Numeric trace with x[n] = 1, 2, 3 at n = 0, 1, 2 (0 elsewhere), and the same input delayed by n₀ = 2:

answer: The last two rows match, as time invariance requires.
Causality. y[n] uses x[n] (present) and x[n − 1] (past), never x[n + 1]. The system is causal. It has memory, because it stores one past sample.

answer.text: BIBO stability. If |x[n]| ≤ M for all n, then by the triangle inequality

answer: Every bounded input gives an output bounded by 2M, so the system is BIBO stable. The LTI test agrees: the impulse response is h[n] = δ[n] + δ[n − 1], and Σ |h[n]| = 1 + 1 = 2, which is finite.

The system is LTI, so it is fully described by its impulse response: h[n] = δ[n] + δ[n − 1], the values 1, 1 at n = 0, 1. Every output is the convolution y[n] = x[n] * h[n]; for the trace above, 1, 2, 3 convolved with 1, 1 gives 1, 3, 5, 3, as found.

The bound 2M is reached: x[n] = M for all n gives y[n] = 2M. An alternating input x[n] = M(−1)ⁿ gives y[n] = M(−1)ⁿ + M(−1)ⁿ⁻¹ = 0, so this system passes slow inputs and blocks the fastest one, a simple low-pass filter.
Conclusion: linear, time-invariant, causal and BIBO stable. Check: with M = 3 in the trace above, the largest output is 5 ≤ 2 × 3 = 6.

bank.q: Use the inner-product definition to test whether x₁(t) = 1 and x₂(t) = cos(2πt) are orthogonal on 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Then state the coefficient formula for expanding a signal in an orthogonal set {φₙ}, and use it to approximate x(t) = t² by c₁x₁(t) + c₂x₂(t).
outline: Inner product ⟨x₁, x₂⟩ = ∫₀¹ cos(2πt) dt
The integral is zero, so the signals are orthogonal
Coefficient cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩/Kₙ with Kₙ = ⟨φₙ, φₙ⟩
For orthonormal φₙ, cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩
Interval, conjugate for complex signals; the approximation and its error

answer.text: Orthogonality test.
answer.pre:
⟨x₁, x₂⟩ = ∫₀¹ 1 · cos(2πt) dt = [sin(2πt)/(2π)] from 0 to 1
         = (sin 2π − sin 0)/(2π) = 0

answer: Both signals are nonzero and the inner product is zero, so x₁ and x₂ are orthogonal on [0, 1]. The interval matters: on [0, 0.5] the same integral is [sin(2πt)/(2π)] from 0 to 0.5 = 0 as well, but on [0, 0.25] it is 1/(2π) ≈ 0.159, not orthogonal.

answer.text: Coefficient formula. For x ≈ Σ cₙφₙ with {φₙ} orthogonal on [a, b], take the inner product with φₘ; all cross terms vanish:
answer.pre: cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩ / Kₙ = (1/Kₙ) ∫ₐᵇ x(t) φₙ*(t) dt,     Kₙ = ∫ₐᵇ |φₙ(t)|² dt

answer: For an orthonormal set every Kₙ = 1 and cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩. For complex signals the second signal is conjugated.

answer.text: Energies of the two members.
answer.pre:
K₁ = ∫₀¹ 1 dt = 1
K₂ = ∫₀¹ cos²(2πt) dt = ∫₀¹ (1 + cos 4πt)/2 dt = 1/2

answer.text: Coefficients for x(t) = t².
Energy bookkeeping.

answer: Meaning of the coefficients: c₁ = 1/3 is the average value of t² over [0, 1], since the constant term of any orthogonal expansion on an interval of length 1 is ∫ x dt. c₂ = 0.1013 measures how much of t² rises and falls like cos(2πt) on [0, 1].

For complex sets the conjugate matters: with φₙ = e<sup>j2πnt</sup> on [0, 1], cₙ = ∫₀¹ x(t) e<sup>−j2πnt</sup> dt, the exponential Fourier coefficient. Dropping the conjugate would give the coefficient of the wrong harmonic.

Check: the kept energy 0.1162 is below the signal energy 0.2, as Bessel's inequality requires. The two members are not a complete set, so error energy remains; adding sin(2πt) and the higher harmonics would drive it towards zero.

bank.q: Explain the analogy between vectors and signals. Derive the best constant c₁₂ for approximating f₁(t) by c₁₂f₂(t) over (t₁, t₂), and apply it to approximate the square wave f(t) = 1 on (0, π), −1 on (π, 2π) by c₁₂ sin t. Find the mean square error.
outline: Component of vector A along B: c = A·B/|B|², error perpendicular to B
Signal version: minimise ε = (1/(t₂ − t₁))∫(f₁ − c f₂)² dt
dε/dc = 0 gives c₁₂ = ∫f₁f₂ dt / ∫f₂² dt
Square wave: c₁₂ = 4/π ≈ 1.273
Mean square error 1 − 8/π² ≈ 0.189; error energy 2π − 16/π ≈ 1.190
answer: Vectors. The component of A along B is cB with c = A·B/|B|². The error e = A − cB is perpendicular to B, and this c gives the shortest error: |A − kB| for any other k is longer.

Signals. On an interval a signal has one component per instant, so the dot product becomes the inner product ⟨f₁, f₂⟩ = ∫ f₁(t) f₂(t) dt and the squared length becomes the energy ‖f₂‖² = ∫ f₂²(t) dt. Approximating f₁ by c f₂ is projecting one vector on another.

answer.text: Derivation. Error fₑ = f₁ − c f₂. Minimise the mean square error over (t₁, t₂):
answer.pre:
ε = (1/(t₂ − t₁)) ∫ [f₁(t) − c f₂(t)]² dt
dε/dc = (1/(t₂ − t₁)) ∫ 2[f₁ − c f₂](−f₂) dt = 0
⇒ ∫ f₁ f₂ dt = c ∫ f₂² dt
⇒ c₁₂ = ∫ f₁(t) f₂(t) dt / ∫ f₂²(t) dt

answer: d²ε/dc² = (2/(t₂ − t₁)) ∫ f₂² dt > 0, so this is a minimum. At the minimum ∫ fₑ f₂ dt = 0: the error is orthogonal to f₂, the perpendicular of the vector picture. If ∫ f₁f₂ dt = 0, then c₁₂ = 0 and the signals are orthogonal.

answer.text: Square wave by sin t over (0, 2π).
answer.pre:
∫ f sin t dt = ∫ sin t dt over (0, π) − ∫ sin t dt over (π, 2π) = 2 + 2 = 4
∫ sin² t dt over (0, 2π) = π
c₁₂ = 4/π ≈ 1.2732

answer.text: Error.
answer.pre:
energy of f        = ∫ 1 dt = 2π ≈ 6.2832
energy kept        = c₁₂² ∫ sin² t dt = (16/π²)(π) = 16/π ≈ 5.0930
error energy       = 2π − 16/π ≈ 1.1902
mean square error  ε = 1.1902/(2π) = 1 − 8/π² ≈ 0.1894

answer.text: Check that 4/π is the minimum. The error energy as a function of c is 2π − 8c + πc²:

answer: A vector check of the same rule: A = (3, 4) and B = (1, 0) give c = A·B/|B|² = 3/1 = 3; the error A − 3B = (0, 4) is perpendicular to B, and its length 4 is the smallest any multiple of B can leave.

With f₂ = sin 3t instead, ∫ f sin 3t dt = 2/3 + 2/3 = 4/3 and ∫ sin² 3t dt = π, so c = 4/(3π) ≈ 0.424: the square wave also has a smaller component along the third harmonic, which the next chapter adds in.
The approximation carries (16/π)/(2π) = 8/π² ≈ 81 % of the energy. The best sine is taller than the square wave (1.27 against 1) because it must make up for being too low near t = 0 and t = π.

bank.q: Compare energy signals and power signals. Show that a periodic signal with finite nonzero power is a power signal, and explain why a finite-energy signal has zero average power.
outline: Energy signal: finite E = ∫|x(t)|²dt
Power signal: finite nonzero P = lim of the average of |x(t)|²
Periodic signal: average power over one period is finite and nonzero
Its total energy over infinite time is infinite
For finite E, P = lim E/T = 0 as T → ∞

answer.text: Definitions.
answer.pre:
E = ∫ |x(t)|² dt  over all t
P = lim (T → ∞) (1/T) ∫ |x(t)|² dt,  over −T/2 ≤ t ≤ T/2

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Feature
Energy signal
Power signal
rows: dies out or lasts a finite time
a sinusoid, a periodic square wave, a dc level

answer.text: Periodic signal → power signal. Let x have period T₀ and energy per period E₀ = ∫ |x|² dt over one period, with 0 < E₀ < ∞. Take a window holding k whole periods, T = kT₀:
answer.pre:
P = lim (k → ∞) (k E₀)/(k T₀) = E₀/T₀       finite and nonzero
E = lim (k → ∞) k E₀ = ∞

answer: Partial periods at the window edges add at most E₀ to the integral and vanish after dividing by T. So P = E₀/T₀, the average over one period, and E = ∞: the signal is a power signal.

Numbers: x(t) = 4 cos(100πt) + 2 V has T₀ = 0.02 s and P = 4²/2 + 2² = 12 W, so E₀ = P × T₀ = 0.24 J per period. After 50 periods (1 s) the energy is 12 J, after 5000 periods 1200 J: it grows without bound.

answer.text: Finite energy → zero power. If E is finite, the integral over any window is at most E:

answer: Numbers: a pulse of 2 V lasting 2 s has E = 2² × 2 = 8 J. Over a 100 s window the average is 8/100 = 0.08 W; over 10 000 s it is 0.0008 W, heading to 0.
Hence no signal can be both: E finite forces P = 0, and P > 0 forces E = ∞. Some signals are neither, such as the ramp r(t) = t u(t), whose energy and average power are both infinite.
A signal that is neither: the ramp r(t) = t u(t) gives ∫ t² dt over 0 to T/2 = T³/24 inside a window of length T, so the average T²/24 grows without bound and E = ∞ as well.
Check: 12 W × 1 s = 12 J, matching 50 periods × 0.24 J.

bank.q: Analyse how the order of time shifting and time scaling affects the graph of x(3t − 6). Give two correct sequences of operations and one wrong sequence, with sketches described.
outline: Write x(3t − 6) = x(3(t − 2))
Correct order 1: scale by 3, then shift right by 2
Correct order 2: shift right by 6, then scale by 3
Wrong order: shift right by 2, then scale by 3, gives x(3t − 2)
Describe the position and width at each step
answer: Use the pulse x(t) = 2 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 s (0 elsewhere) so every sketch has numbers.

answer.text: Target. The nonzero part of x(3t − 6):

answer: So y(t) = x(3t − 6) is a pulse of height 2 on 2 to 2.667 s, width 2/3 s. Rewriting x(3t − 6) = x(3(t − 2)) shows a delay of b/a = 6/3 = 2 s after compression.
Correct order 1: scale, then shift by b/a. x(t) → x(3t): the pulse on 0 to 2/3 s. Then replace t by t − 2: x(3(t − 2)) = x(3t − 6), the pulse on 2 to 2.667 s.

Correct order 2: shift by b, then scale. x(t) → x(t − 6): the pulse on 6 to 8 s. Then replace t by 3t: x(3t − 6), the pulse on 6/3 to 8/3 = 2 to 2.667 s. Compression about t = 0 divides both edges by 3, which is why a shift of 6 ends up as 2.
Wrong order: shift by b/a, then scale. x(t) → x(t − 2) on 2 to 4 s, then t → 3t gives x(3t − 2) on 2/3 to 4/3 s. The compression shrinks the shift a second time.
Another wrong order: scale, then shift by b. x(3t) then t → t − 6 gives x(3(t − 6)) = x(3t − 18) on 6 to 6.667 s.

answer.text: Summary of the sketches (all of height 2):

answer: Sketch description: four rows on one time axis from 0 to 9 s, each a rectangle of height 2. Row 1 (the target) on 2 to 2.667 s. Row 2, x(3t), on 0 to 0.667 s. Row 3, x(t − 6), on 6 to 8 s. Row 4, the wrong x(3t − 2), on 0.667 to 1.333 s. The two correct routes end on the same rectangle; the wrong one sits 1.333 s too early.

Rule: after scaling, shift by b/a; before scaling, shift by b. Check: at t = 2.5 s the argument 3(2.5) − 6 = 1.5 lies in 0 to 2, so y(2.5) = 2; at t = 1 s the argument is −3, so y(1) = 0, which rules out the wrong sketch on 0.667 to 1.333 s.

bank.q: Evaluate the statement: 'A causal system is always stable, and a linear system is always time-invariant.' Give definitions and counterexamples or reasoning.
outline: Causality: output depends on present and past inputs only
Stability: every bounded input gives a bounded output
Counterexample causal but unstable: y(t) = e<sup>t</sup>x(t)
Linearity: superposition holds
Counterexample linear but time-varying: y(t) = t x(t)
Conclusion: both claims are false; the properties are independent
answer: Definitions. Causal: y at time t depends only on x at times ≤ t. BIBO stable: |x(t)| ≤ Mᵢₙ for all t implies |y(t)| ≤ Mₒᵤₜ for all t, with Mₒᵤₜ finite. Linear: T{a x₁ + b x₂} = a T{x₁} + b T{x₂}. Time-invariant: x(t − t₀) gives y(t − t₀) for every t₀.

Claim 1: causal ⇒ stable. False. Take y(t) = etx(t). It uses only x(t), so it is causal. With the bounded input x(t) = 1, y(t) = et: y(5) = 148.4 and y(10) = 22 026, with no bound. Causal but unstable.

A second counterexample, from LTI theory: the integrator y(t) = ∫ x(τ) dτ over τ ≤ t has h(t) = u(t). It is causal because h(t) = 0 for t < 0, but ∫ |h(t)| dt = ∞, and the input u(t) gives the ramp r(t), which grows without bound.

Claim 2: linear ⇒ time-invariant. False. Take y(t) = t x(t). Superposition holds, so it is linear. With x(t) = 2 V and t₀ = 1 s, at t = 2 s: T{x(t − 1)} = 2 × 2 = 4 V·s, but y(t − 1) = (2 − 1) × 2 = 2 V·s. Linear but time-varying.
The converse claims fail too. y(t) = x(t + 1) is stable (|y| ≤ Mᵢₙ) but noncausal. y(t) = x²(t) is time-invariant but nonlinear: doubling the input quadruples the output.

answer.text: Property table for the four systems:

answer: Check the last row: input x = 3 gives 9, input 6 gives 36 ≠ 2 × 9, so x² is not linear; a delayed input gives a delayed square, so it is time-invariant; a bounded |x| ≤ M gives |y| ≤ M².

For LTI systems the two properties are two different conditions on the impulse response: causal when h(t) = 0 for t < 0, stable when ∫ |h(t)| dt is finite. h(t) = e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t) meets both (∫ |h| dt = 0.5); h(t) = u(t) is causal but ∫ |h| dt = ∞; h(t) = e<sup>−2|t|</sup> has ∫ |h| dt = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1, so it is stable, but it is nonzero for t < 0, so it is noncausal. Neither condition implies the other.

Verdict. Both parts of the statement are false. Linearity, time invariance, causality and stability are four independent questions; each must be tested from its own definition, and one counterexample is enough to fail a property.

bank.q: An orthogonal set {φ₁, φ₂, φ₃, …} is used to represent a signal x(t) on an interval. Derive the coefficient formula, state Parseval's relation, and explain what completeness means for exact representation.
outline: Inner product ⟨x, φₙ⟩ = ∫x(t)φₙ*(t)dt
Coefficient cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩/Kₙ
For an orthonormal set, cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩
Parseval: energy = Σ|cₙ|²Kₙ
Completeness: the error energy tends to zero for every finite-energy signal; no nonzero signal is orthogonal to the whole set
answer: Setting. {φₙ} is orthogonal on [a, b]: ⟨φₘ, φₙ⟩ = ∫ₐᵇ φₘ(t)φₙ*(t) dt = 0 for m ≠ n, and Kₙ = ⟨φₙ, φₙ⟩ > 0. We want x(t) ≈ Σ cₙφₙ(t).

answer.text: Coefficient formula. Take the inner product of both sides with φₘ:
answer.pre:
⟨x, φₘ⟩ = Σ cₙ ⟨φₙ, φₘ⟩ = cₘ Kₘ     (every n ≠ m term is zero)
⇒ cₘ = ⟨x, φₘ⟩ / Kₘ = (1/Kₘ) ∫ₐᵇ x(t) φₘ*(t) dt

answer: For an orthonormal set (Kₙ = 1), cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩. These coefficients also minimise the error energy, and each one is found without the others.

answer.text: Error energy with N terms. Expanding |x − Σ cₙφₙ|² and using orthogonality:
answer.pre: ε(N) = ∫ₐᵇ |x(t)|² dt − Σ |cₙ|² Kₙ      (n = 1 to N)

answer: So Σ |cₙ|²Kₙ ≤ E for every N (Bessel's inequality), and each extra term lowers the error by |cₙ|²Kₙ.

Completeness. The set is complete when ε(N) → 0 as N → ∞ for every finite-energy x on [a, b]; equivalently, no nonzero signal is orthogonal to every φₙ. Then x = Σ cₙφₙ exactly in energy (it may differ at isolated points such as jumps).

answer.text: Parseval's relation (complete set):
answer.pre: ∫ₐᵇ |x(t)|² dt = Σ |cₙ|² Kₙ      (orthonormal: Σ |cₙ|²)

answer.text: Worked check with the shifted Legendre set on [0, 1]: φ₁ = 1, φ₂ = 2t − 1, φ₃ = 6t² − 6t + 1 (K = 1, 1/3, 1/5) and x(t) = t², whose energy is ∫₀¹ t⁴ dt = 1/5.

answer: The error falls 0.0889 → 0.0056 → 0, and 1/9 + 1/12 + 1/180 = 36/180 = 1/5 = E: Parseval holds. If only two members were available, Bessel's inequality 0.1944 ≤ 0.2 would hold but 1/180 of the energy would be missing.
Orthonormal version: dividing each member by √Kₙ gives ψₙ = φₙ/√Kₙ, for example √3(2t − 1) on [0, 1]. The coefficients become dₙ = cₙ√Kₙ and Parseval reads E = Σ |dₙ|².

The Fourier series is the most used case: the exponential set e<sup>jnω₀t</sup> on one period has Kₙ = T₀, so Dₙ = (1/T₀) ∫ x(t) e<sup>−jnω₀t</sup> dt and Parseval becomes the power relation (1/T₀) ∫ |x|² dt = Σ |Dₙ|².

Evaluation. Orthogonality makes the coefficients easy; completeness is what guarantees that the representation is exact. An incomplete set can still represent some signals exactly (the sines on (0, 2π) for an odd square wave), but it fails for others (cos t has all sine coefficients zero).

bank.q: Show that sin nt and sin mt (m ≠ n) are orthogonal on (0, 2π). Expand the square wave f(t) = 1 on (0, π), −1 on (π, 2π) in the set {sin nt}, tabulate the energy captured as terms are added, find how many nonzero terms are needed for 95 % of the energy, and explain whether the sine set is complete.
outline: ∫ sin nt sin mt dt = 0 for m ≠ n; Kₙ = π
cₙ = 4/(nπ) for odd n, 0 for even n
Term energy 16/(n²π); running total against 2π
95 % needs five nonzero terms (n = 1 to 9): 95.96 %, while four give 94.96 %
Parseval check with Σ 1/n² = π²/8 over odd n; cos t shows the sines alone are not complete

answer.text: Orthogonality. Use the product-to-sum identity:
answer.pre:
sin nt sin mt = [cos(n − m)t − cos(n + m)t]/2
∫ sin nt sin mt dt over (0, 2π) = 0 − 0 = 0     for m ≠ n (whole periods of each cosine)
Kₙ = ∫ sin² nt dt = ∫ (1 − cos 2nt)/2 dt = π

answer.text: Coefficients.
answer.pre:
⟨f, sin nt⟩ = ∫ sin nt dt over (0, π) − ∫ sin nt dt over (π, 2π)
           = (1 − cos nπ)/n + (1 − cos nπ)/n = 2(1 − cos nπ)/n
odd n:  4/n  ⇒ cₙ = 4/(nπ)
even n: 0    ⇒ cₙ = 0

answer: So f(t) = (4/π)(sin t + sin 3t/3 + sin 5t/5 + …) on (0, 2π). The energy of f is E = ∫ 1 dt = 2π ≈ 6.2832, and term n carries cₙ²Kₙ = (16/(n²π²))π = 16/(n²π).

answer.text: Energy captured.

answer: 95 % of the energy. Four nonzero terms (n = 1, 3, 5, 7) give 94.96 %, just short. The fifth, n = 9, brings 95.96 %. So five nonzero terms are needed.
Parseval check. Σ cₙ²Kₙ = (16/π) Σ 1/n² over odd n = (16/π)(π²/8) = 2π = E. The error energy (last column) falls towards zero, so the sine set represents this square wave exactly in energy.
Pointwise behaviour. At t = π every term sin nπ = 0, so the series gives 0, the midpoint of the jump from +1 to −1. The equality is in energy, not at every point.

Is the sine set complete on (0, 2π)? No. Test with g(t) = cos t: ⟨cos t, sin nt⟩ = ∫ cos t sin nt dt = 0 for every n ≥ 1 over (0, 2π), so all its coefficients are zero and the error energy stays at ∫ cos² t dt = π for every N. The square wave worked only because it is odd about t = π, as every sine is. Adding the constant 1 and the cosines cos nt gives the trigonometric Fourier set, which is complete on any interval of length 2π.

Power form of the same check: if the square wave repeats with T₀ = 2π, its average power is 2π/2π = 1 W. Parseval for the sine series gives Σ cₙ²/2 = Σ 8/(n²π²) over odd n = (8/π²)(π²/8) = 1 W, the same value.
The first two terms already carry 90.06 % of the energy; the higher harmonics carry little energy and mainly sharpen the corners and the jumps of the square wave.
Check: the n = 1 row repeats the single-sine approximation f ≈ (4/π) sin t, whose error energy 2π − 16/π = 1.1902 is the first entry of the last column.

glossary.def: A function of an independent variable that carries information.
An operator that maps an input signal to an output signal.
The quantity on which a signal depends, usually time t or integer index n.
The value or strength of a signal at a chosen point or its peak scale.
A signal defined for every real value of time t.
A signal defined only at integer index n.
Each value x[n] of a discrete-time signal; for a sampled signal it is x(nTₛ).
A signal whose total energy E=∫|x(t)|²dt is finite.
A signal whose average power is finite and nonzero.
A signal that satisfies x(t+T)=x(t) for all t with some T>0.
The smallest positive T for which a periodic signal repeats.
A signal that satisfies x(−t)=x(t).
A signal that satisfies x(−t)=−x(t).
A generalized signal with zero width, unit area, and zero value except at the origin.
A signal that is zero before the origin and one from the origin on (u(0) = 1 in this book).
A signal that is zero before the origin and rises linearly after it.
A signal of the form A·exp(st), where s may be real or complex.
A change x(t)→x(t−t₀) that moves a signal in time.
A change x(t)→x(at) that compresses or stretches a signal in time.
A change x(t)→x(−t) that flips a signal about the origin.
A system that obeys superposition for all inputs and constants.
A system whose response does not depend on the absolute time of the input.
A system whose output does not depend on future input values.
A system in which every bounded input produces a bounded output.
For signals, ⟨x,y⟩=∫x(t)y*(t)dt; it measures similarity and projection.
Signals whose inner product is zero on the chosen interval.
sgn(t) = 1 for t > 0 and −1 for t < 0; sgn(t) = 2u(t) − 1 except at t = 0.
sinc(t) = sin(πt)/(πt), with sinc(0) = 1 and zeros at nonzero integers; some books use sin(t)/t instead.
An orthogonal set whose N-term error energy tends to zero for every finite-energy signal on the interval.
For a complete orthogonal set, the energy of a signal equals Σ |cₙ|²Kₙ, the sum of the energies of its components.
